- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peak by 5–10% if followed by a spike.
- If model shows strong upward momentum (e.g., 3+ consecutive rising forecasts) and sentiment is neutral or bearish, cap forecast growth to avoid overshoot.
- After a sharp price spike, model often overcorrects downward; if sentiment is bearish post-spike, reduce forecast decline by 5–10% to avoid premature bottoming.
- When sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and model forecasts are rising, apply a downward bias correction — subtract 2–5% from forecast if sentiment remains negative.
- If model forecast mean is significantly above true outcome mean (e.g., >10% over 30d), apply a “mean reversion” adjustment: reduce forecast by 1–3% per day if sentiment is neutral or mixed.
- For short-term (1–7d) forecasts, model often overreacts to sentiment shifts; use sentiment lag (e.g., 2–3d) to smooth out sudden directional changes.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles, model tends to misalign with sentiment direction — adjust forecast to match sentiment’s recent trend direction, not its peak.
